summaries.example: Imagine a spinning lamp shining a spot on a wall. The beam of light travels from the lamp to the wall, so it can carry a change, such as a red color added by a filter. The moving spot on the wall cannot carry that change around the wall. Salmon used this kind of example to help explain the difference between a real causal process and something that only looks like one.
summaries.summary: Wesley Salmon was a philosopher of science who asked how people can reason carefully when they do not have complete certainty. He studied probability, induction, confirmation, explanation, causation, rational thinking, and scientific realism. Induction means using patterns in observed cases to make predictions about unobserved cases. Salmon favored a frequency-based approach: probability is connected with how often events occur in suitable groups. He also argued that explaining something is not merely giving an argument that shows it happened. A real explanation should identify relevant factors and, especially, the causal processes or mechanisms that produced the event. Salmon used examples such as a barometer and a storm to show that prediction and explanation can differ. A falling barometer may predict a storm, but the change in air pressure helps explain both. His work also explored how evidence can support theories about unobserved entities, such as atoms and molecules.
key_ideas: Wesley Salmon studied how science uses probability, evidence, causes, and explanations.
He thought induction is important because science often uses what has happened before to make predictions.
Salmon connected probability with frequencies: how often something happens in a group of similar cases.
He argued that a good explanation should point to relevant factors and, when possible, to the causes or mechanisms involved.
He believed scientific ideas about things we cannot directly see, such as atoms, can be supported by evidence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Science often must make decisions with incomplete information. Salmon’s ideas help us ask whether evidence is relevant, whether a prediction is the same as an explanation, and whether a proposed cause really produces an effect. These questions matter whenever people use observations to understand the world.

important_terms.definition: A way of learning from many observed cases to make a careful guess about cases we have not seen.
A measure used to describe how often something happens or how strongly evidence supports a possibility.
A group of similar cases used when deciding how likely a particular event is.
A connection in which one event or process helps bring about another.
An ongoing thing in space and time that can carry information, structure, or causal influence.

questions_to_think_about: When is it reasonable to use past events to guess what will happen next?
Can something help us predict an event without explaining why it happened?
What makes two cases similar enough to belong in the same group?
How could evidence support belief in something that cannot be seen directly?

summaries.example: Suppose a barometer falls shortly before storms. The fall is statistically relevant to a storm, so it can help predict one. But the barometer does not cause the storm. A drop in atmospheric pressure is a better causal explanation because it helps account for both the barometer reading and the storm. Salmon used cases like this to distinguish statistical relevance from causal relevance.
summaries.summary: Wesley Salmon’s philosophy of science centers on the problem of how uncertain evidence can support prediction, explanation, and rational action. In probability, he defended a frequency-oriented approach. Probabilities are tied to frequencies in reference classes, and single-case judgments require selecting classes that are homogeneous with respect to relevant properties. Salmon considered induction unavoidable in science, but he did not claim that it could be justified by deduction. Instead, he pursued a pragmatic vindication: induction is needed for extending knowledge and making predictions. He examined Reichenbach’s attempt to justify an inductive rule and proposed requirements such as normalization and linguistic invariance, later exploring the relationship between discovery and justification. In confirmation theory, Salmon distinguished absolute confirmation from incremental confirmation and favored an objective Bayesian approach in which prior probabilities are constrained by empirical considerations rather than being merely personal degrees of belief. In his theory of explanation, Salmon criticized the idea that an explanation is simply an argument. Statistical relevance can improve prediction, but explanation also requires causal information. His account developed from the Statistical-Relevance model toward a mechanistic view involving causal processes, interactions, and conserved quantities. He called this an ontic conception because explanations concern how events fit into the world’s causal structure. Salmon also argued that empiricism and scientific realism can be compatible: patterns of observable evidence may support hypotheses about unobservable entities when those hypotheses explain regularities through common causes.
key_ideas: Salmon developed a probabilistic empiricism while also defending realism about theoretical entities.
He treated induction as necessary for science but accepted that its justification cannot be a purely deductive proof.
His objective Bayesianism allowed prior probabilities to be informed by empirical considerations such as simplicity, symmetry, analogy, and past success.
The Statistical-Relevance model sought to identify factors that change an event’s probability, while causal explanation sought the mechanisms responsible for its occurrence.
Salmon distinguished conjunctive forks, where a common cause screens off correlations, from interactive forks, where effects remain statistically connected because of an interaction.
He eventually treated statistical relevance and causal-process information as complementary levels of explanation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Salmon’s work connects several questions that are often separated: How should probability be interpreted? How can induction be defended? What makes evidence confirm a theory? What distinguishes prediction from explanation? His answers influenced later discussions of probabilistic causation, mechanisms, scientific realism, and the philosophy of science more broadly.

important_terms.definition: Inference from observed cases to unobserved or future cases; Salmon regarded it as indispensable to scientific method.
An interpretation of probability that relates probability to frequencies in an appropriate, sufficiently homogeneous reference class.
A class selected to include cases relevantly similar to the case whose probability is being assessed.
Evidence that changes the probability of a hypothesis, as distinct from making it highly probable in an absolute sense.
A relation in which conditioning on one factor removes the statistical connection between two other factors.
A continuous spatiotemporal entity capable of transmitting information, structure, or causal influence.
Salmon’s view that explanation concerns how events fit into physical mechanisms operating in the world.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a successful prediction fail to count as an explanation?
Can induction be practically justified even if it cannot be logically proved reliable?
What makes a reference class appropriately homogeneous rather than merely convenient?
Why might a common cause explain a correlation between two events?
Should explanations focus mainly on patterns in data, mechanisms in the world, or both?

summaries.example: Two children at the same party become sick with the same illness. It may look as if one child caused the other’s illness, but suppose neither infected the other. Their shared exposure to an already sick child could be a common cause. The common cause helps explain why the two illnesses happened together, while the simple correlation between them does not by itself show which event caused which.
summaries.summary: Wesley Salmon was a major philosopher of science who examined how evidence supports scientific beliefs and actions. He worked in an empiricist tradition, emphasizing experience, but he also defended scientific realism—the view that successful scientific theories may describe real but unobservable entities. Salmon treated probability as closely connected to frequency. To estimate the probability of a particular event, we need a reference class containing cases relevantly similar to it. This is difficult because we may not know all the properties that matter. Salmon also defended induction, the practice of moving from observed cases to predictions about unobserved ones. He accepted that Hume’s challenge shows induction cannot receive a simple logical proof, so he explored a practical justification based on its role in extending knowledge and guiding action. Salmon’s work on confirmation distinguished evidence that raises a hypothesis’s probability from evidence that makes it highly probable overall. In explanation, he challenged the view that explaining is just presenting an argument. His Statistical-Relevance model focused on factors that alter probabilities, while his causal approach focused on mechanisms and processes. The difference can be seen in the barometer example: a falling barometer may predict a storm, but atmospheric pressure helps explain the storm. Salmon also studied common causes, causal interactions, and processes that transmit information or conserved quantities. His views changed in response to criticism, and he ultimately gave both statistical and causal information an important role.
key_ideas: Salmon saw probability and induction as central to scientific reasoning.
He supported a frequency view of probability, while recognizing difficulties in choosing the right reference class for a single case.
He thought the problem of induction is real: past success does not logically guarantee future success.
He distinguished statistical relevance from causation; a correlation may help prediction without identifying the true cause.
His explanation theory combined information about relevant patterns with information about causal mechanisms.
He defended the possibility that evidence can support realistic theories about unobservable scientific entities.
summaries.why_it_matters: Salmon’s questions appear whenever people interpret evidence. They help us separate “these things happen together” from “this caused that,” and “this theory predicts well” from “this theory explains how the event happened.” His work also shows that philosophical ideas can change as arguments and criticisms reveal new problems.

important_terms.definition: Using patterns from things already observed to form expectations about things not yet observed.
A number describing how likely an event is, often connected with how frequently similar events occur.
A carefully chosen group of similar cases used to estimate the probability of an event.
Evidence that is connected with an outcome because it changes the outcome’s probability.
A cause that helps explain why two events are connected, even though one event did not cause the other.
A continuing thing or event that can carry a change, signal, or influence from one place and time to another.

questions_to_think_about: If a pattern has worked many times, what gives us reason to expect it to work again?
How could choosing a different reference class change a probability estimate?
Why is a correlation not always a cause?
What extra information does a causal explanation provide beyond a prediction?
Can scientists reasonably believe in things they cannot observe directly?
